- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) and forecast is flat or rising slowly, model tends to underreact — increase forecast slightly to capture sentiment-driven momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) and forecast is rising, model often overestimates — reduce forecast slope or cap upward movement.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots — apply a “cool-down” correction: reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 3–5 days.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline after peak), model often fails to adjust — add a “reversion buffer” to forecast, especially if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If sentiment history is mostly 0.0 and forecast is trending upward, model often overestimates — cap forecast at 1–2% above recent 7-day average to avoid overconfidence.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >5% from 30-day moving average of history, adjust forecast to align with recent volatility — don’t assume linear continuation.
